Bandwidth on this part is not a function of footprint alone: §2.3 measured a
GEMM gaining up to 1.6x purely from moving an operand's row stride 256 B off
a power-of-two. But the `bandwidth` family only ever measures a contiguous
sweep, so the 805/236 GB/s ceilings it reports are best-case figures a
strided kernel does not automatically get, and a GEMM cannot separate the
stride from its own tiling.

**Built**: `shaders/strided_read.comp` + `bench/ops_stride.go`, run as the
`stride` family. The access pattern is `rows` rows of which the first
`rowBytes` are touched, spaced `stride` bytes apart; every touched 16-byte
chunk is read exactly once in every variant, so the byte set, the footprint
and the number of `buffer_load_b128`s are identical across the sweep and
only two things vary:

- **the stride**, which adds a gap and changes nothing about what is read —
  exactly what padding a real matrix's leading dimension does, including
  that the pad bytes are never read;
- **the request shape**, via `LANES_PER_ROW`: how many consecutive 16-byte
  chunks of one row go to consecutive lanes, so one 64-lane load spans
  `64/LANES_PER_ROW` distinct rows. 1 row is a contiguous 1 KB sweep; 64
  rows is the 64-address/16-bytes-each gather; 32 rows is the shape a 16×16
  fp16 `coopMatLoad` actually issues.

Each case is checked against a host-computed checksum over its (row, chunk)
set — derived from the geometry, deliberately not from the shader's lane
mapping — so a variant that covered a chunk twice or skipped one would fail
rather than report a plausible bandwidth.

### Two mechanisms, and the big one is not the one §2.3 found

**1. Channel coverage — up to 4x, and it hits a contiguous read as hard as a
gather.** The interleave on this part is 256 B over **sixteen** channels,
i.e. a **4 KB rotation** (which is what a 256-bit LPDDR5X bus of 16-bit
sub-channels gives). Row *k* starts at `k*stride`, so row starts land only on
the multiples of `g = gcd(stride, 4096)` inside one rotation, and each row
covers `rowBytes` bytes from its start. If `rowBytes < g` the union of them
**misses whole channels**, and the achievable fraction of peak is exactly the
fraction of channels touched:

> **coverage = min(1, rowBytes / gcd(stride, 4096))**

which held to within 2% at every point measured. At 1024 B rows, 64 MiB
touched (GB/s; `model` is the formula above, and the rows are requests
spanning 1..64 distinct rows):

| rows/req | 1024 | 1280 | 2048 | 3072 | 4096 | 6144 | 8192 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **model** | 1.00 | 1.00 | **0.50** | 1.00 | **0.25** | **0.50** | **0.25** |
| 1 (contiguous) | 243 | 216 | 120 | 216 | 60 | 118 | 57 |
| 4 | 243 | 240 | 122 | 239 | 58 | 119 | 57 |
| 16 | 234 | 236 | 113 | 226 | 55 | 115 | 57 |
| 32 | 230 | 232 | 113 | 229 | 58 | 114 | 58 |
| 64 (gather) | 232 | 240 | 116 | 229 | 59 | 116 | 57 |

Note which strides are bad: 2048 and 4096 and 8192 — the ones a tidy
allocator picks — while 1280 and 3072 are perfect. This effect is invisible
to everything §2.3 measured, because a K=4096 fp16 row is 8192 B, already
≥ any `g`, so its coverage is full at every stride.

**2. Per-request aliasing — up to 1.34x, and it needs a gather.** With
coverage full (8192 B rows), a stride that is a multiple of 4 KB costs a
contiguous read *nothing* and costs progressively more as one request spans
more rows. 64 MiB touched, 8192 B rows, GB/s:

| rows/req | 8192* | 8208 | 8256 | 8320 | 8448 | 8704 | 9216 | 10240 | 12288* | 16384* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (contiguous) | 242 | 238 | 238 | 240 | 242 | 243 | 243 | 243 | 242 | 243 |
| 4 | 231 | 225 | 227 | 230 | 236 | 241 | 243 | 245 | 232 | 232 |
| 16 | 205 | 210 | 216 | 230 | 236 | 237 | 237 | 238 | 202 | 202 |
| 32 | 202 | 205 | 215 | 237 | 234 | 235 | 237 | 237 | 201 | 200 |
| 64 (gather) | **181** | 197 | 221 | 236 | 230 | 233 | **239** | 235 | **174** | **181** |

(* = multiple of 4 KB. Identical to within 1% at 256 MiB touched, so this is
a DRAM-level effect and not a footprint one.)

**The period is 4 KB, not the 2 KB §2.3 inferred**, and the nine-point sweep
says so unambiguously: 10240 and 14336 *are* multiples of 2 KB and run at the
full rate (235-237 GB/s for the 64-row gather), while 8192, 12288 and 16384 —
the multiples of 4 KB — are the only slow strides in the sweep.

**The MALL is immune to both.** At 16 MiB touched every stride and every
shape delivers ~782 GB/s, with the unpadded 64-row gather the single
exception at 0.95x. So the engine has to pad what it streams and can ignore
the stride of anything it keeps cache-resident.

### The answer to (b) retires §2.3's open question

At a de-aliased stride, a 64-address gather reads at **239 GB/s against a
contiguous sweep's 243** — within 2%, over identical bytes. **Request shape
costs essentially nothing on this memory system once the stride is right.**
Two consequences:

- The [N,K] layout a real `Linear` weight already has is **fully usable
  above MALL size**; there is no bandwidth reason to transpose weights at
  load time.
- The residue §2.3 could not explain — transposed-B still 1.6x behind
  row-major at N=4096 *with both strides padded* — is **not** a
  memory-request-shape effect, which was the leading candidate. §2.3 ruled
  out request count and cache-line survival; this rules out the shape of the
  requests themselves. Whatever is left is in the kernel, not in the bus.

### Engine rules, all three free

1. **Pad every row-major tensor's leading dimension to 256 B past a multiple
   of 4 KB.** That single rule satisfies both mechanisms at once: its
   `gcd(stride, 4096)` is 256, so coverage is full for any row of ≥256 B,
   and the stride is off the 4 KB multiple, so the gathers de-alias. Costs
   256 B per row — 3% at K=4096 fp16, and it is the rule §2.3 already
   derived, now with the right period and a reason that covers every shape.
2. **Never round a row stride up to a page.** A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
   (2048 B rows) aligned to 4096 B reads at **half** this chip's DRAM
   bandwidth; 1024 B rows at an 8192 B stride, a **quarter**. This is the
   largest free loss the suite has turned up, and it is one a tidy allocator
   inflicts on itself while looking like it is doing the right thing.
3. **Do not over-pad.** Recovery is complete by +128-256 B and then flat
   across a whole period, so more pad buys nothing and costs footprint —
   which is what made §2.3's GEMM sweep appear to *decline* past +256 B.

## Next steps (pick up here)

`IDEAS.md` has the full backlog with its "Suggested order of attack"
updated for what §0, §1.1, §2.1 and §2.3 found. In short:

1. **IDEAS §5.1b — the strided-bandwidth probe, which is §2.3's unfinished
   half.** Two questions, one microbenchmark, both engine-wide rather than
   kernel-specific: (a) what a channel-aliased stride costs at constant
   footprint — only the 256 B/2 KB case has been measured, on one kernel,
   and the engine needs the shape of that curve to pad every allocation;
   (b) what the machine delivers for one 16-address/16-bytes-each gather
   versus a contiguous sweep of the same bytes at the same stride — the
   shape question left by the 1.6x transposed-B still loses at N=4096, and
   the thing a GEMM measurement cannot separate from tiling. It decides
   whether the [N,K] layout a real `Linear` weight already has is usable
   above MALL size.
   The `bandwidth` family only ever measures contiguous streaming, so its
   805/236 GB/s ceilings are best-case figures a strided kernel does not
   automatically get.
2. **IDEAS §2.4 — workgroup swizzle.** Still the cheapest structural item,
   but restate the premise before building it: §2.3 pushed the AI-32
   kernels to 742-887 GB/s of *implied* MALL traffic, past the 805 GB/s
   ceiling, so they are not simply MALL-pinned and some of that traffic is
   being served by the L1s. The sharp test is that a swizzle should help
   the AI-32 kernels and do nothing for the AI-85 variant (306 GB/s
   implied).
3. **Pad the strides in the other kernels.** GEMV, W4A8 and W8A8 all index
   weights by a power-of-two row stride, none has a stride push constant,
   and none has been measured against a padded one. §2.3 makes this cheap
   to try and hard to justify skipping — though note decode is already at
   89% of the DRAM bus, so the headroom there is small by construction.
4. **IDEAS §2.2's int8 arm — a `PRECISION_I8` variant of
   `gemm_wmma.comp`**, accumulating in int32. Small change to a kernel that
   now reaches 45% of the ceiling, halves its operand bytes, and gives W8A8
   prefill its number. (The *Q4*-unpack version stays downgraded: there is
   no int8 matrix-rate bonus on this chip, and the winning kernel has no LDS
   tile whose fill cost a cheaper unpack would improve.)
5. **IDEAS §1.3 — wide loads on the other GEMV kernels.** Measured at 1.17x
   on W4A8. fp16 GEMV sits at 75% of its DRAM ceiling and W8A8 at 73%,
   where W4A8 now reaches 89%.
6. **IDEAS §1.2 — remove the runtime integer divisions** (`pc.N / pc.block`
   and `n / pc.block`) from everything W4A8 did not rewrite: the
   naive/tiled GEMM paths and the old quantized GEMV variants.
   `gemv,naive,q4` is still slower than naive fp32, which is the symptom.
7. **IDEAS §6.2 — wave32 vs wave64**, now more interesting than when it was
   filed: WMMA is natively a 16x16x16 wave32 shape, RADV runs these shaders
   at wave64, and §2.1's tile size is capped by the 256-VGPR wave64 limit
   rather than by occupancy. Needs a small `vk/shim.c` change to pass
   `VK_EXT_subgroup_size_control`'s `requiredSubgroupSize`.
8. **IDEAS §1.6 — the activation-quantize cost W8A8 and W4A8 both hide.**
   Both kernels get `x` quantized on the host, outside the timed loop, and
   W4A8 additionally gets its per-block activation sums for free. A real
   decode step must produce both on-GPU between layers. The sums are one
   extra reduction over N (cheap, and fusable into the quantize pass), but
   it should be measured rather than assumed — it is the one place where
   these numbers are friendlier than production would be.
9. **Still open from §0**: CPU-side submit/fence cost (the half of §4.1 the
   `overhead` family does not measure), and the last ISA question from §6.1

   survives warming — in GEMV it does not.

   and the new rows), `cmd/probe/main.go`, plus `IDEAS.md`, `README.md`,

1	# strix-halo-vulkan
2	
3	A Go + Vulkan compute harness for exploring shaders on the Strix Halo iGPU
4	(gfx1151 / AMD Radeon 8060S, RADV driver), plus a benchmark suite
5	(`cmd/bench`) that measures the operations neural-network inference is
6	built from — GEMM, GEMV, elementwise/activation, softmax/RMSNorm — across
7	the implementation "flavours" that matter on this hardware: naive vs.
8	shared-memory-tiled vs. subgroup-reduced vs. cooperative-matrix
9	(`VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`, RDNA3.5's matrix-multiply accelerator), and
10	fp32 vs. fp16 vs. quantized (int8/int4, GGML-style block scales) weights vs.
11	W8A8 and W4A8 (int8 or 4-bit weights against int8 activations, reduced via
12	`VK_KHR_shader_integer_dot_product`'s packed-dot instructions).
13	
14	Two kernels here are the current answers for the two shapes inference comes
15	in. For **decode** (GEMV, memory-bound), **W4A8**
16	(`shaders/gemv_w4a8.comp`): 4-bit weights fed to the packed-int8 dot
17	instruction through its mixed-signedness overload, at **819 GFLOP/s and 211
18	GB/s against DRAM-resident weights — 89% of this machine's 236 GB/s memory
19	bandwidth**, 2.4x the int8-weight kernel it replaces. For **prefill** (GEMM,
20	compute-bound), the register-blocked cooperative-matrix GEMM
21	(`shaders/gemm_wmma.comp`): **28.4 TFLOP/s, 51% of this chip's measured
22	55.5 TFLOP/s of matrix-core throughput** (26.0 TFLOP/s at N=4096), 6.2x the
23	straightforward coopmat kernel it replaces at that shape. The last 1.13x of
24	that came from neither tiling nor instruction selection but from *operand
25	strides*: every fragment load in a WMMA GEMM is K-strided, a power-of-two
26	leading dimension aims all the addresses of one load at the same memory
27	channel, and padding each stride 256 B off a 4 KB multiple — a host-side
28	allocation change — is worth up to 1.35x on the kernels that were already
29	winning and 2.6x on the [N,K] weight layout.
30	
31	The `stride` family then measured that memory system directly
32	(`shaders/strided_read.comp`) and found a second, larger effect with no
33	kernel-side cause at all: channel interleave on this part is 256 B across
34	sixteen channels, so a row shorter than `gcd(stride, 4096)` bytes **never
35	addresses some of them**, and the achievable fraction of DRAM bandwidth is
36	exactly `min(1, rowBytes/gcd(stride, 4096))`. A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
37	whose rows were aligned to 4 KB reads at **half** this chip's bandwidth; 1 KB
38	rows at an 8 KB stride, a **quarter** — and unlike the aliasing above this
39	hits a plainly contiguous read as hard as a gather. Pad every row stride to
40	256 B past a multiple of 4 KB and both effects go away. `IDEAS.md` explains
41	how each kernel gets where it is and what is still on the table.
42	
43	No third-party Go modules — `go.mod` has no dependencies. Vulkan access is a
44	hand-written cgo binding straight against the system Vulkan loader
45	(`vulkan/vulkan.h` + `libvulkan.so`), with the struct-heavy parts of the
46	Vulkan API built in a small C shim (`vk/shim.c`/`vk/shim.h`) rather than Go,
47	since cgo forbids passing a Go struct across the boundary when one of its
48	fields is itself a pointer into other Go memory — and Vulkan's
49	`*CreateInfo` structs are built almost entirely out of such chains.
50	
51	## Layout
52	
53	- `vk/` — the engine: `shim.c`/`shim.h` do the actual Vulkan calls
54	  (instance/device setup with optional fp16/int8/cooperative-matrix device
55	  features, buffer allocation preferring device-local+host-visible memory,
56	  N-buffer pipeline creation with push constants and specialization
57	  constants, GPU-timestamp-timed dispatch); `engine.go` is the idiomatic Go
58	  wrapper (`Instance`, `Device`, `Buffer`, `ShaderModule`, `ComputePipeline`).
59	- `main.go` — the original demo: picks the Strix Halo iGPU, uploads a float
60	  array, runs `shaders/double.comp`, reads it back, verifies it.
61	- `shaders/*.comp` — the compute shaders (GLSL); `shaders/shaders.go`
62	  embeds their compiled SPIR-V via `go:embed`. Precision/tile-size variants
63	  of the same source are generated via `glslc -D` flags, not duplicated GLSL.
64	- `cmd/probe/main.go` — dispatches a single `.spv` once, so
65	  `RADV_DEBUG=asm` / `RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats` can be pointed at any shader to
66	  read its disassembly or its VGPR/LDS/spill counts. Compilation-time
67	  questions only; it binds dummy buffers and computes nothing meaningful.
68	- `bench/` — the benchmark harness: GPU-timestamp-based timing
69	  (`bench.go`), fp16/int8/int4 quantization helpers matching GGML-style
70	  block scales (`quant.go`), clock/power instrumentation (`sysmon.go`), and
71	  one file per op family (`ops_*.go`) wiring shader variants + buffer
72	  layouts + a CPU-reference correctness check to a size sweep.
73	- `cmd/bench/main.go` — the benchmark CLI.
74	
75	## Requirements
76	
77	- Go, gcc/clang, `pkg-config`
78	- Vulkan loader + headers (`vulkan-icd-loader`, `vulkan-headers` on Arch)
79	- `glslc` (from `shaderc`) to compile shaders — only needed when a `.comp`
80	  file changes, not to build/run the Go programs themselves.
81	
82	## Usage
83	
84	```sh
85	go generate ./...   # only needed after editing a .comp file
86	go build ./...
87	
88	./strix-halo-vulkan   # original demo
89	
90	go run ./cmd/bench    # benchmark suite; see -h for flags (sizes, blocks,
91	                      # warmup/iters, -csv output, -skip op families)
92	```
93	
94	`cmd/bench` prints a results table per op family and, with `-csv`, writes
95	`op,variant,weight_format,block_size,size,ns_per_iter,gflops,gbps` rows,
96	followed by `sclk_mhz,sclk_mhz_min,sclk_mhz_max,power_w,detail`, for further
97	analysis (e.g. "which quantization block size + matrix shape wins").
98	
99	## Reading the numbers honestly
100	
101	Four op families exist to keep the rest of the suite interpretable. They
102	are cheap to run and worth running first.
103	
104	- **`peak`** measures the hardware's instruction-issue ceilings with kernels
105	  whose operands are register-resident before the loop, so nothing in the
106	  timed loop touches memory (`shaders/alu_peak.comp`): scalar fp32 FMA,
107	  packed-fp16 FMA, `dotPacked4x8` (int8 packed dot), and cooperative-matrix
108	  fp16 and int8. Every other kernel's GFLOP/s should be read as a fraction
109	  of the relevant one of these — not of a spec-sheet figure extrapolated
110	  from a different chip. `-cus` (default 40) expresses each ceiling as
111	  ops/clock/CU, the form comparable against published RDNA3 figures.
112	- **`overhead`** measures a shader that does nothing, isolating the cost of
113	  a dispatch plus the pipeline barrier between iterations from any real
114	  work. It bounds how much a long chain of small kernels (decode) can lose
115	  to launch cost, and explains bandwidth measurements at sizes small enough
116	  to be dominated by a fixed cost.
117	- **`stride`** measures what the memory system delivers for a *fixed* set of
118	  bytes as the row stride and the request shape vary — the qualifier on
119	  `bandwidth`, which only ever measures a contiguous sweep and therefore
120	  reports best-case ceilings a strided kernel does not automatically get. One
121	  kernel (`shaders/strided_read.comp`) reads every touched 16-byte chunk
122	  exactly once in every variant, so the byte set and the load count are
123	  identical and only the stride and the lane→address mapping change;
124	  `LANES_PER_ROW` sets how many consecutive chunks of a row go to
125	  consecutive lanes, so one request spans 1 row (contiguous) up to 64 rows (a
126	  gather). `-stridepads`, `-striderowbytes` and `-stridefootprints` set the
127	  three sweeps; the printed grid carries a `model` row giving
128	  `min(1, rowBytes/gcd(stride, 4096))`, which the measurements track to
129	  within 2%. Each case is checked against a host checksum over its (row,
130	  chunk) set, so a mis-derived index fails instead of reporting a plausible
131	  bandwidth.
132	- **`gemv_cold`** measures the decode-shape GEMV against weights several
133	  times larger than the last-level cache. The square `gemv` sweep's largest

### This session: IDEAS §5.1b — the strided-bandwidth probe

`IDEAS.md` §5.1b asked for the memory system to be measured directly instead
of inferred through a GEMM: fixed bytes touched, sweeping (a) the stride
against the channel-interleave period and (b) request *shape* at constant
stride. **Both are answered, and there turned out to be two mechanisms
rather than one — the larger of which nothing in the suite was looking for,
because it needs no gather and no kernel at all to trigger.**

**New code:**
- `shaders/strided_read.comp` — reads `rows` rows of which the first
  `rowBytes` are touched, spaced `stride` bytes apart, one `uvec4`
  (`buffer_load_b128`) per lane. Every touched chunk is read exactly once in
  every variant, so the byte set, the footprint and the load-instruction
  count are identical across the whole sweep and only two things move: the
  stride (a push constant) and the lane→address mapping. `LANES_PER_ROW`
  sets the latter — how many consecutive 16-byte chunks of one row go to
  consecutive lanes — so one 64-lane request spans `64/LANES_PER_ROW`
  distinct rows: 1 (a contiguous 1 KB sweep) through 64 (a 64-address,
  16-bytes-each gather), with 32 being the shape a 16×16 fp16 `coopMatLoad`
  issues. Five variants, one `-D` apart.
- `bench/ops_stride.go` — the `stride` family: three sweeps (row length ×
  touched footprint × stride), `PrintStrideSummary`'s pivot grid, and
  `strideChannelCoverage`, the closed-form model below, printed as a `model`
  row so each grid checks itself against it.
- `bench/ops_stride.go` verifies every case against a host checksum over its
  (row, chunk) set, computed from the geometry and deliberately *not* from
  the shader's lane mapping — so a mapping that read a chunk twice or skipped
  one fails instead of reporting a plausible bandwidth. It caught nothing,
  which is the point: without it a bandwidth number is unfalsifiable.
- `vk/engine.go` gains `Buffer.ReadUint32` and `Buffer.MappedPointer` (the
  latter to fill a 128 MiB buffer in place rather than via a host-side copy).
- `cmd/bench/main.go` gains `-stridepads`, `-striderowbytes`,
  `-stridefootprints` and the `stride` skip name.

**Finding 1 — channel coverage, worth 2-4x, and it hits contiguous reads.**
The interleave is 256 B across **sixteen** channels, a 4 KB rotation. Row *k*
starts at `k*stride`, so row starts land only on multiples of
`g = gcd(stride, 4096)`, and each row covers `rowBytes` from its start. When
`rowBytes < g` the union **never addresses some channels**, and the

**[measured] §2.3 added a second axis to this family and one specific probe
it should own. That probe is now built, and it found two mechanisms rather
than one — the larger of which nothing in the suite was looking for, because
it needs neither a gather nor a kernel to trigger.**

§2.3 measured a GEMM gaining up to 1.6x purely from moving an operand's row
stride 256 B off a power-of-two, but the `bandwidth` family only ever
measures a contiguous sweep, so the 805/236 GB/s ceilings it reports are
best-case figures a strided kernel does not automatically get — and a GEMM
cannot separate the stride from its own tiling.

**Built**: `shaders/strided_read.comp` + `bench/ops_stride.go`, run as the
`stride` family. The pattern is `rows` rows of which the first `rowBytes`
are touched, spaced `stride` bytes apart, one `uvec4` per lane. Every
touched 16-byte chunk is read exactly once in every variant, so the byte
set, the footprint and the number of `buffer_load_b128`s are identical
across the sweep and only two things move:

- **the stride**, which adds a gap and changes nothing about what is read —
  exactly what padding a real matrix's leading dimension does, including
  that the pad bytes are never read;
- **the request shape**, via `LANES_PER_ROW`: how many consecutive 16-byte
  chunks of one row go to consecutive lanes, so one 64-lane load spans
  `64/LANES_PER_ROW` distinct rows. 1 row is a contiguous 1 KB sweep, 64
  rows is the 64-address/16-bytes-each gather, 32 rows is what a 16×16 fp16
  `coopMatLoad` issues.

Each case is checked against a host checksum over its (row, chunk) set,
computed from the geometry and deliberately *not* from the shader's lane
mapping, so a variant that covered a chunk twice or skipped one fails
instead of reporting a plausible bandwidth.

#### Mechanism 1: channel coverage — 2-4x, and it hits contiguous reads

The interleave on this part is 256 B across **sixteen** channels, i.e. a
**4 KB rotation** (what a 256-bit LPDDR5X bus of 16-bit sub-channels gives).
Row *k* starts at `k*stride`, so row starts land only on the multiples of
`g = gcd(stride, 4096)` inside one rotation, and each row covers `rowBytes`
from its start. When `rowBytes < g` the union of them **never addresses some
channels at all**, and the achievable fraction of peak is exactly the
fraction of channels touched:

> **coverage = min(1, rowBytes / gcd(stride, 4096))**

1024 B rows, 64 MiB touched, GB/s (`model` is the formula; rows are how many
distinct rows one request spans):

| rows/req | 1024 | 1280 | 2048 | 3072 | 4096* | 5120 | 9216 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **model** | 1.00 | 1.00 | **0.50** | 1.00 | **0.25** | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 1 (contiguous) | 243 | 241 | **120** | 242 | **61** | 245 | 239 |
| 4 | 243 | 241 | 122 | 243 | 61 | 245 | 239 |
| 16 | 234 | 238 | 113 | 233 | 55 | 237 | 231 |
| 32 | 230 | 239 | 113 | 234 | 58 | 238 | 232 |
| 64 (gather) | 232 | 240 | 120 | 237 | 59 | 242 | 235 |

The model holds to within 2% at every point, for every shape. Note which
strides are the bad ones — 2048, 4096, 8192, the ones a tidy allocator picks
— while 1280 and 3072 are perfect. At 2048 B rows (a K=1024 fp16 weight row)
it is the same law one notch weaker: 243 GB/s at stride 2048, **123 at 4096**,
242 at 6144, **121 at 8192**.

None of this is visible to anything §2.3 measured: a K=4096 fp16 row is
8192 B, already ≥ any `g`, so its coverage is full at every stride.

#### Mechanism 2: per-request aliasing — up to 1.32x, and it needs a gather

With coverage full (8192 B rows), a stride that is a multiple of 4 KB costs a
contiguous read *nothing* and costs progressively more the more rows one
request spans. 64 MiB touched, GB/s:

| rows/req | 8192* | 8208 | 8256 | 8320 | 8448 | 8704 | 9216 | 10240 | 11264 | 12288* | 14336 | 16384* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (contiguous) | 243 | 238 | 238 | 240 | 242 | 243 | 244 | 244 | 243 | 242 | 243 | 243 |
| 4 | 231 | 226 | 228 | 230 | 236 | 240 | 244 | 245 | 242 | 232 | 245 | 233 |
| 16 | 205 | 210 | 216 | 229 | 236 | 237 | 237 | 238 | 236 | 202 | 236 | 202 |
| 32 | 204 | 205 | 214 | 238 | 235 | 236 | 238 | 238 | 236 | 201 | 236 | 200 |
| 64 (gather) | **182** | 198 | 230 | 237 | 230 | 233 | **239** | 237 | 238 | **174** | 238 | **180** |

(* = multiple of 4 KB. Identical to within 1% at 256 MiB touched, so this is
a property of DRAM and not of the footprint.)

**The period is 4 KB, not the 2 KB §2.3 inferred.** With nine strides inside
one rotation the sweep is unambiguous: 10240 and 14336 **are** multiples of
2 KB and run at the full rate, while 8192, 12288 and 16384 — the multiples of
4 KB — are the only slow strides. And recovery inside a period is complete by
+128-256 B, then flat: +16 B gets a third of it, +64 B most of it, and
everything from +128 B to +3072 B is within noise of the best.

#### The MALL behaves differently on both counts

At 16 MiB touched a pure read delivers **940-965 GB/s** — above the 805 GB/s
§0.4 measured with a read+write copy — and:

- it is **immune to the gather penalty**: the 64-row gather measures 824-896
  GB/s at *every* stride, aliased or not, i.e. a flat ~0.93x of the other
  shapes rather than §2.3's 1.32x spread;
- it is **more exposed to coverage**: at 1024 B rows and a 4096 B stride it
  collapses to 59 GB/s — 0.06x, far below the model's 0.25x, and *below* the
  DRAM figure for the same pattern. Slicing the cache by the same address
  bits shrinks its effective capacity to a quarter, so a 16 MiB working set
  that fits comfortably at a good stride does not fit at all at a bad one.
  The 0.50x cases land at 0.44-0.53x, on the model.

One MALL-resident oddity is reproducible and unexplained: the *purest*
pattern — the fully contiguous shape at zero pad, i.e. a plain linear sweep —
measures **782 GB/s in all three row-length groups** while every perturbed
stride of the same shape reaches 848-966. It is the one cell where adding a
pad helps a contiguous read, it came out at exactly 782 three times in the
committed run, and two earlier runs put it at 794-839 twice and 942 once. If
it is real it is a cross-wave phasing effect, which is exactly what the
follow-up below is about. Cache-resident numbers here carry ~10% one-sided
scatter in any case (see `strideBatches`).

#### The answer to (b) retires §2.3's open question

At a de-aliased stride a 64-address gather reads at **239 GB/s against a
contiguous sweep's 244** — within 2%, over identical bytes. **Request shape
costs essentially nothing once the stride is right.** So:

- The [N,K] layout a real `Linear` weight already has is **fully usable above
  MALL size**; there is no bandwidth reason to transpose weights at load
  time.
- The residue §2.3 could not explain — transposed-B still 1.6x behind
  row-major at N=4096 *with both strides padded* — is **not** a
  memory-request-shape effect, which was the leading candidate. §2.3 ruled
  out request count and cache-line survival; this rules out request shape.
  What is left is in the kernel, not the bus.

Worth carrying: the *bus* penalty for an aliased stride is at most 1.32x and
only for a gather, while §2.3's kernel lost 1.63x to it — a GEMM **amplifies**
the bandwidth penalty rather than merely inheriting it.

#### Engine rules, all three free

1. **Pad every row-major tensor's leading dimension to 256 B past a multiple
   of 4 KB.** One rule covers both mechanisms: `gcd(stride, 4096)` becomes
   256, so coverage is full for any row of ≥256 B, and the stride is off the
   4 KB multiple, so gathers de-alias. 256 B per row — 3% at K=4096 fp16.
2. **Never round a row stride up to a page.** A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
   aligned to 4096 B reads at **half** this chip's DRAM bandwidth; 1024 B
   rows at an 8192 B stride, a **quarter**. This is the largest free loss the
   suite has found, and it is one a tidy allocator inflicts on itself while
   looking like it is doing the right thing.
3. **Do not over-pad.** Recovery is complete by +128-256 B and then flat, so
   more pad buys nothing and costs footprint — which is what made §2.3's
   GEMM sweep appear to *decline* past +256 B (see the correction there).

**Effort**: low (done). **Value**: high (delivered) — the probe was written
to quantify a 1.35x and found a 2-4x cliff next to it.

**What this leaves open**, and it is now the sharpest item in the file: every
shape here varies the addresses inside *one* request, and the contiguous
shape deliberately walks along a row, so **consecutive waves are never a
stride apart**. That is exactly the GEMV/W4A8 pattern — one wave per row,
contiguous within it, rows 8192 B apart — and §2.3 found the cross-request
stride was what mattered for the LDS staging loads ("what matters is the
address stride across the concurrent loads, not which instruction issues
them"). The 782 GB/s oddity above is a hint that it is real. One `-D` on
`strided_read.comp` swaps the traversal so consecutive waves start on
consecutive rows; that is the whole experiment, and W4A8's 89% of the bus
bounds what it can be worth for decode at 1.12x.

**Also still open from this item** is its original half: deliberately

per-expert MoE weights, a blocked GEMM B-panel). Unaffected by the above,
except that the MALL's indifference to request shape makes it slightly more
attractive and its sensitivity to coverage slightly more dangerous.

content.content:
**§2.3's contradiction is now resolved, and resolving it was worth more than
the layout question that raised it.** The cause is DRAM channel aliasing:
every fragment load in these kernels is K-strided, a power-of-two leading
dimension puts all 16 addresses of one load in the same channel, and the
penalty is periodic in the stride with a 2 KB period. Padding each operand's
leading dimension 256 B off a multiple of 2 KB — a host-side allocation
change, no shader restructuring — is worth 1.6x on the transposed-B kernel,
**up to 1.35x on the kernels that already won**, and takes the suite's best
GEMM to **28.4 TFLOP/s (51% of the WMMA ceiling)**. It also retires the
"pinned at the MALL's 805 GB/s" reading of §2.1's plateau. See §2.3.

=== 158-170
   did **not** matter — LDS staging, more waves per workgroup, and the
   occupancy floor below were all irrelevant or harmful here.
   **[measured] §2.3 then found a second, independent lever that is not
   arithmetic intensity at all: operand *stride*.** Every fragment load in
   these kernels is K-strided, and a power-of-two leading dimension puts all
   16 of its addresses in one memory channel; padding each stride 256 B off
   a 2 KB multiple is worth 0-5% at N=4096, 4-35% at N=2048 and 2.6x on the
   [N,K] weight layout, for a new best of 28.4 TFLOP/s (51%). It also breaks
   the "pinned at 760 GB/s" reading above: the de-aliased AI-32 kernels
   imply 742-887 GB/s of MALL traffic, i.e. at or *past* the 805 GB/s
   ceiling, so the L1s must be absorbing part of what that arithmetic
   attributes to the MALL — and the AI-85 plateau at 26.0 TFLOP/s implies
   only 306 GB/s, so whatever binds it is not bandwidth at any level.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='IDEAS.md'
s=open(p).read()
a='''1. **Pad every row-major tensor's leading dimension to 256 B past a multiple
   of 4 KB.** One rule covers both mechanisms: `gcd(stride, 4096)` becomes
   256, so coverage is full for any row of ≥256 B, and the stride is off the
   4 KB multiple, so gathers de-alias. 256 B per row — 3% at K=4096 fp16.
2. **Never round a row stride up to a page.** A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
   aligned to 4096 B reads at **half** this chip's DRAM bandwidth; 1024 B
   rows at an 8192 B stride, a **quarter**. This is the largest free loss the
   suite has found, and it is one a tidy allocator inflicts on itself while
   looking like it is doing the right thing.
3. **Do not over-pad.** Recovery is complete by +128-256 B and then flat, so
   more pad buys nothing and costs footprint — which is what made §2.3's
   GEMM sweep appear to *decline* past +256 B (see the correction there).'''
assert a in s
b='''1. **Pad every row-major tensor's leading dimension to 256 B past a multiple
   of 4 KB.** One rule covers both mechanisms: `gcd(stride, 4096)` becomes
   256, so coverage is full for any row of ≥256 B, and the stride is off the
   4 KB multiple, so gathers de-alias. 256 B per row — 3% at K=4096 fp16.
2. **Never round a row stride up to a page.** A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
   aligned to 4096 B reads at **half** this chip's DRAM bandwidth; 1024 B
   rows at an 8192 B stride, a **quarter**. It is a loss a tidy allocator
   inflicts on itself while looking like it is doing the right thing.
3. **Do not over-pad.** Recovery is complete by +128-256 B and then flat, so
   more pad buys nothing and costs footprint — which is what made §2.3's
   GEMM sweep appear to *decline* past +256 B (see the correction there).

Two corollaries of the coverage law worth stating on their own, because they
decide where rule 1 actually earns its 3%:

- **A densely packed tensor is never at risk.** If `stride == rowBytes` then
  `gcd(stride, 4096) ≤ rowBytes` for *any* row length, so coverage is 1 by
  construction. This mechanism does not exist until something introduces a
  gap — which means it is created by padding, and only by *badly chosen*
  padding. It is also why every kernel in the suite that streams a whole
  dense matrix has been fine all along, W4A8 at 89% of the bus included.
- **But any kernel that reads a *strip* of a larger tensor is exposed, and
  that is what tiling is.** A blocked GEMM that sweeps a 1 KB-wide panel of a
  K=4096 fp16 matrix has `rowBytes` 1024 against a stride of 8192, so
  `gcd` is 4096 and coverage is **0.25** — a quarter of DRAM bandwidth, for a
  kernel doing nothing wrong except tiling. Padding that matrix's stride to
  8448 restores coverage to 1 for *every* panel width (its `gcd` is 256).
  This is the same (rowBytes, gcd) regime as the measured 1024 B/4096 B point
  above, not an extrapolation from it. It also makes rule 1 a prerequisite
  for §2.4 and for the MALL-blocking half of this item rather than a 3%
  optimisation: block a panel out of an unpadded weight matrix and the
  blocking can cost more than it saves.'''

content.text: The MALL data is richer than I'd written: coverage penalties there depend on span too. Correcting that section with the full picture:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='IDEAS.md'
s=open(p).read()
a='''At 16 MiB touched a pure read delivers **940-965 GB/s** — above the 805 GB/s
§0.4 measured with a read+write copy — and:

- it is **immune to the gather penalty**: the 64-row gather measures 824-896
  GB/s at *every* stride, aliased or not, i.e. a flat ~0.93x of the other
  shapes rather than §2.3's 1.32x spread;
- it is **more exposed to coverage**: at 1024 B rows and a 4096 B stride it
  collapses to 59 GB/s — 0.06x, far below the model's 0.25x, and *below* the
  DRAM figure for the same pattern. Slicing the cache by the same address
  bits shrinks its effective capacity to a quarter, so a 16 MiB working set
  that fits comfortably at a good stride does not fit at all at a bad one.
  The 0.50x cases land at 0.44-0.53x, on the model.'''
assert a in s
b='''At 16 MiB touched a pure read delivers **930-965 GB/s** — above the 805 GB/s
§0.4 measured with a read+write copy — and:

- it is **immune to the gather penalty**: the 64-row gather measures 824-896
  GB/s at *every* stride, aliased or not, i.e. a flat ~0.93x of the other
  shapes rather than DRAM's 1.32x spread;
- **the coverage law does not carry over to it**, and what replaces it is not
  yet pinned down. Six cases at 16 MiB touched, all with the same bytes read:

  | row | stride | coverage | span | measured |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1024 B | 3072 / 5120 / 9216 | 1.00 | 48-144 MiB | 780-968 (MALL) |
  | 2048 B | 2048 | 1.00 | 16 MiB | 782-945 (MALL) |
  | 2048 B | 4096 | 0.50 | 32 MiB | 769-924 (**MALL, no penalty**) |
  | 1024 B | 2048 | 0.50 | 32 MiB | 353-469 (**halfway**) |
  | 2048 B | 8192 | 0.50 | 64 MiB | 118-121 (DRAM × 0.50) |
  | 1024 B | 4096 | 0.25 | 64 MiB | 55-61 (DRAM × 0.25) |

  Read down it: **full coverage keeps the set resident however far it is
  spread** — a 16 MiB working set scattered over a 144 MiB span still gets
  MALL bandwidth, which is worth knowing on its own. **Partial coverage keeps
  it only while the span is also inside 32 MiB**, and past that the DRAM law
  reappears undiminished. The one case that is neither (1024 B rows, 2048 B
  stride: partial coverage, 32 MiB span) lands halfway. The plausible reading
  is that the address bits selecting a channel also select a cache slice, so
  partial coverage concentrates the touched lines onto a fraction of the sets
  and shrinks the effective capacity — but that is inference, and pinning it
  needs its own experiment: a footprint sweep at a fixed bad stride, which
  the `stride` family can already run from flags.

  Note the direction of the engine consequence: **§5.1b's own "keep it under
  32 MiB for 3.4x" premise only holds for a fully-covering access pattern.**
  A blocked panel with a bad stride does not get the MALL either.'''
s=s.replace(a,b,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')
PY

content.text:
Done. The next item in `IDEAS.md` was **§5.1b's strided-bandwidth probe** — §2.3's unfinished half. It's built, run, and documented, and it found more than the item asked for.

## What I built

- **`shaders/strided_read.comp`** (5 variants, one `-D` apart) — reads `rows` rows of which the first `rowBytes` are touched, spaced `stride` apart. Every touched 16-byte chunk is read exactly once in every variant, so the byte set, footprint and load-instruction count are identical and only the stride and the lane→address mapping move. `LANES_PER_ROW` sets how many rows one 64-lane request spans: 1 (contiguous 1 KB sweep) → 64 (a 64-address gather).
- **`bench/ops_stride.go`** — the `stride` family, three sweeps, a pivot grid that prints a self-checking `model` row, and a host checksum per case derived from the geometry rather than from the shader's mapping.
- Flags `-stridepads`/`-striderowbytes`/`-stridefootprints`; `vk.Buffer.ReadUint32`/`MappedPointer`; `results.csv` regenerated (1129 rows, 360 of them new).

## What it found

**Two mechanisms, not one — and the bigger one needs no gather at all.**

1. **Channel coverage, worth 2-4x.** The interleave is 256 B over **sixteen** channels (a 4 KB rotation). Row starts land only on multiples of `g = gcd(stride, 4096)`, so a row shorter than `g` leaves whole channels unaddressed: `coverage = min(1, rowBytes/g)`, matching measurement to within 2% at every point, *including for a plainly contiguous read*. A K=1024 fp16 matrix with rows aligned to 4 KB reads at half the bus; 1 KB rows at an 8 KB stride, a quarter.
2. **Per-request aliasing, worth up to 1.32x** — §2.3's effect, and it needs a multi-row request: 182 GB/s for a 64-row gather at stride 8192 vs 239 de-aliased, while the contiguous shape is flat at 243 everywhere.

**Corrections to previously recorded conclusions:** the period is **4 KB, not 2 KB** (10240 and 14336 are 2 KB multiples and run at full rate); §2.3's apparent optimum-then-decline was a de-aliasing step times a growing footprint, since its B operand crosses the MALL as the pad grows. **Request shape is free** once the stride is right (gather within 2% of contiguous), which retires the leading candidate for §2.3's unexplained residue and means the `[N,K]` weight layout needs no transpose.

Two corollaries I'd flag as the practically important part: a *densely packed* tensor is never at risk (`stride == rowBytes` forces full coverage), so this is a hazard created by padding — but any kernel reading a **strip** of a larger tensor is exposed, which is what tiling is. A 1 KB-wide panel of a K=4096 fp16 matrix gets a quarter of the bus, and padding the stride to 8448 fixes it for every panel width. That makes the padding rule a prerequisite for the §2.4/§3.3 blocking work rather than a 3% tweak.

## Caveats I've recorded rather than papered over

- The MALL doesn't follow the coverage law; its behaviour depends on span as well, one case lands halfway, and the mechanism there is **inferred, not measured**. I filed the footprint sweep that would settle it as the next item (it runs from existing flags).
- One reproducible oddity is unexplained: the purest linear sweep measures 782 GB/s where perturbed strides reach 805-966.
- The probe does **not** cover concurrent-but-contiguous requests from *different* waves at an aliased stride — which is exactly the GEMV/W4A8 pattern. That's now the top next item; it's one `-D` away.
- Mid-session, an orphaned `exe/bench` from a killed run competed for the GPU and put ~10% of cache-resident cases at 0.3-0.5x. I re-ran everything clean; `pkill -f cmd/bench` does not kill `go run`'s child, and a pattern matching your own shell kills the shell first. Both the lesson and the resulting `strideBatches`/batch-length changes are documented.

`IDEAS.md`, `TODO.md` and `README.md` are updated throughout (including the roofline table, which now carries a dagger on both bandwidth rows). Everything builds clean; nothing is committed.
